claim: Voltage sensors are integral membrane proteins that 'sense' transmembrane voltage differences.
source: Voltage sensors are integral membrane proteins that 'sense' transmembrane voltage differences.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about voltage sensors.

claim: Voltage sensors exist as regulatory domains on voltage-gated ion channels and voltage-dependent phosphatase enzymes.
source: They exist as regulatory domains on voltage-gated ion channels and voltage-dependent phosphatase enzymes (Hille, 2001; Murata et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hille, 2001 and Murata et al., 2005.

claim: All voltage sensors have a shared structure consisting of four helical transmembrane segments.
source: All voltage sensors have a shared structure consisting of four helical transmembrane segments (Noda et al., 1984; Papazian et al., 1987; Tanabe et al., 1987; Tempel et al., 1987; Jiang et al., 2003a).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations documenting this structural feature.

claim: The fourth helix (S4) contains positive-charged amino acids that move within the transmembrane electrical field as part of a global conformational change.
source: The fourth helix, termed S4, contains positive-charged amino acids that move within the transmembrane electrical field as part of a global conformational change (Noda et al., 1984; Tanabe et al., 1987; Tempel et al., 1987; Aggarwal and MacKinnon, 1996; Seoh et al., 1996; Long et al., 2005a; Long et al., 2005b; Long et al., 2007; Swartz, 2008; Tao et al., 2010; Guo et al., 2016; Shen et al., 2017; Wisedchaisri et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by extensive citations documenting S4 movement.

claim: Sensor conformational changes are imparted onto the channel or enzyme to regulate activity.
source: Sensor conformational changes are imparted onto the channel or enzyme to regulate activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about voltage sensor function.

claim: Nature employs two topologically distinct connections between the voltage sensors and the ion channel pore.
source: Atomic structures of several different eukaryotic voltage-gated K+ (Kv) channels demonstrate that nature employs two topologically distinct connections between the voltage sensors and the ion channel pore (Long et al., 2005a; Whicher and MacKinnon, 2016; Sun and MacKinnon, 2017; Tao et al., 2017; Wang and MacKinnon, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Kv channels are four-fold symmetric, exhibiting one central pore surrounded by four voltage sensors.
source: Viewed down an axis perpendicular to the membrane, Kv channels are four-fold symmetric, exhibiting one central pore surrounded by four voltage sensors.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about Kv channels.

claim: Each subunit encodes a voltage sensor from transmembrane helices S1-S4 and one fourth of the pore from S5 and S6.
source: Each subunit encodes a voltage sensor from transmembrane helices S1-S4 and one fourth of the pore from S5 and S6.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about Kv channel subunit composition.

claim: The channel tetramer is held together by a 'barrel stave' assemblage of the pore, with the voltage sensors residing on the periphery.
source: The channel tetramer is held together by a 'barrel stave' assemblage of the pore, with the voltage sensors residing on the periphery (Long et al., 2005a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Long et al., 2005a.

claim: In domain-swapped Kv channels, the voltage sensor of subunit A leans against the pore-forming helices of subunit B, B against C and so on around the tetramer.
source: If four K+ channel subunits are designated A, B, C and D, to be domain-swapped means the voltage sensor of subunit A leans against the pore-forming helices of subunit B, B against C and so on around the tetramer, as shown in Figure 1A.
evidence: Defined in text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: In non-domain-swapped Kv channels, the voltage sensor of subunit A leans against the pore-forming helices of subunit A, B against B, etc.
source: In non-domain-swapped Kv channels, the voltage sensor of subunit A leans against the pore-forming helices of subunit A, B against B, etc., as shown in Figure 1B.
evidence: Defined in text and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Kv1-7 channels have domain-swapped voltage sensors.
source: Kv1-7 channels have domain-swapped voltage sensors; Kv10-12 and Slo1 channels have non-domain-swapped voltage sensors (Long et al., 2005a; Whicher and MacKinnon, 2016; Sun and MacKinnon, 2017; Tao et al., 2017; Wang and MacKinnon, 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to structural studies.

claim: Kv10-12 and Slo1 channels have non-domain-swapped voltage sensors.
source: Kv1-7 channels have domain-swapped voltage sensors; Kv10-12 and Slo1 channels have non-domain-swapped voltage sensors (Long et al., 2005a; Whicher and MacKinnon, 2016; Sun and MacKinnon, 2017; Tao et al., 2017; Wang and MacKinnon, 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to structural studies.

claim: Voltage-gated Na+ (Nav) and Ca2+ (Cav) channels and other cation channels have domain-swapped voltage sensors.
source: Other voltage-gated channels can also be characterized according to this classification: voltage-gated Na+ (Nav) and Ca2+ (Cav) channels and other cation channels have domain-swapped voltage sensors (Payandeh et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2012; Guo et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2016; Shen et al., 2017; Yan et al., 2017; She et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to structural studies.

claim: HCN channels, which are hyperpolarization-activated cation channels, have non-domain-swapped voltage sensors.
source: HCN channels, which are hyperpolarization-activated cation channels, have non-domain-swapped voltage sensors (Lee and MacKinnon, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee and MacKinnon, 2017.

claim: In domain-swapped channels, the voltage sensor is connected to the pore by an ~20 Å long S4-S5 linker helix.
source: In the former case, the voltage sensor is connected to the pore by an ~20 Å long S4-S5 linker helix, which runs along the channel's cytoplasmic surface and contacts the S6 helix, which forms the gate (Figure 1C) (Long et al., 2005a; Long et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: The S4-S5 linker helix runs along the channel's cytoplasmic surface and contacts the S6 helix, which forms the gate.
source: In the former case, the voltage sensor is connected to the pore by an ~20 Å long S4-S5 linker helix, which runs along the channel's cytoplasmic surface and contacts the S6 helix, which forms the gate (Figure 1C) (Long et al., 2005a; Long et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Conformational changes within the voltage sensor are transmitted to the gate through the S4-S5 linker helix in domain-swapped channels.
source: Conformational changes within the voltage sensor are transmitted to the gate through the S4-S5 linker helix (Long et al., 2005b; Guo et al., 2016; Wisedchaisri et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Channels with non-domain-swapped voltage sensors do not have a helical S4-S5 linker.
source: Channels with non-domain-swapped voltage sensors do not have a helical S4-S5 linker and the mechanism of gate control is unknown (Figure 1D).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: The mechanism of gate control in non-domain-swapped voltage sensors is unknown.
source: Channels with non-domain-swapped voltage sensors do not have a helical S4-S5 linker and the mechanism of gate control is unknown (Figure 1D).
evidence: Explicitly stated as unknown.

claim: KvAP is a Kv channel from the thermophilic archaea Aeropyrum pernix.
source: KvAP is a Kv channel from the thermophilic archaea Aeropyrum pernix (Ruta et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ruta et al., 2003.

claim: KvAP provided the first atomic structures from a voltage-gated ion channel.
source: It provided the first atomic structures from a voltage-gated ion channel and the isolated voltage sensor structure turned out to be the prototype for this domain family (Jiang et al., 2003a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2003a.

claim: The isolated voltage sensor structure of KvAP is the prototype for the voltage sensor domain family.
source: It provided the first atomic structures from a voltage-gated ion channel and the isolated voltage sensor structure turned out to be the prototype for this domain family (Jiang et al., 2003a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2003a.

claim: Crystallographic analysis of the full-length KvAP channel consistently yielded structures with voltage sensors that were rotated relative to the pore and partially unfolded.
source: Crystallographic analysis of the full-length KvAP channel, however, consistently yielded structures with voltage sensors that were rotated relative to the pore and partially unfolded (Jiang et al., 2003a; Lee et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jiang et al., 2003a and Lee et al., 2005.

claim: The KvAP structures led to the proposal of the 'paddle model', in which S4 moves adjacent to the lipid membrane as part of a helix-turn-helix structure consisting of helices S3b and S4.
source: Together with voltage-dependent accessibility measurements, the KvAP structures led us to propose the 'paddle model', in which S4 moves adjacent to the lipid membrane as part of a helix-turn-helix structure consisting of helices S3b and S4 (Jiang et al., 2003b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2003b.

claim: Until recently, all voltage-gated channels were thought to be of the domain-swapped variety.
source: Until recently, all voltage-gated channels were thought to be of the domain-swapped variety (Whicher and MacKinnon, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Whicher and MacKinnon, 2016.

claim: KvAP was considered representative of the more extensively studied Shaker-like (i.e. Kv1) channels, with domain-swapped voltage sensors.
source: For this reason, KvAP was considered representative of the more extensively studied Shaker-like (i.e. Kv1) channels, with domain-swapped voltage sensors (Long et al., 2005a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Long et al., 2005a.

claim: KvAP and the Shaker channel probably undergo rather different voltage-dependent conformational changes when they open.
source: The new structure, together with previous functional data, suggests that KvAP and the Shaker channel, to which KvAP is most often compared, probably undergo rather different voltage-dependent conformational changes when they open.
evidence: This is an inference based on the new structure and previous functional data.

claim: KvAP was expressed in E. coli.
source: KvAP was expressed in E. coli, extracted in a mixture of lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (LMNG) and cholesteryl hemisuccinate (CHS), exchanged into digitonin and then purified as a complex with Fab fragments using size exclusion chromatography (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental procedure.

claim: KvAP was extracted in a mixture of lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (LMNG) and cholesteryl hemisuccinate (CHS).
source: KvAP was expressed in E. coli, extracted in a mixture of lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (LMNG) and cholesteryl hemisuccinate (CHS), exchanged into digitonin and then purified as a complex with Fab fragments using size exclusion chromatography (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental procedure.

claim: KvAP was exchanged into digitonin.
source: KvAP was expressed in E. coli, extracted in a mixture of lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (LMNG) and cholesteryl hemisuccinate (CHS), exchanged into digitonin and then purified as a complex with Fab fragments using size exclusion chromatography (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental procedure.

claim: KvAP was purified as a complex with Fab fragments using size exclusion chromatography.
source: KvAP was expressed in E. coli, extracted in a mixture of lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (LMNG) and cholesteryl hemisuccinate (CHS), exchanged into digitonin and then purified as a complex with Fab fragments using size exclusion chromatography (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental procedure, with supporting figure.

claim: The Fab fragments bind to KvAP's voltage sensors.
source: The Fab fragments, which bind to KvAP's voltage sensors, were used to assist the alignment of channels in image processing.
evidence: This is stated as a known property of the Fab fragments used.

claim: The Fab fragments were used to assist the alignment of channels in image processing.
source: The Fab fragments, which bind to KvAP's voltage sensors, were used to assist the alignment of channels in image processing.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental procedure.

claim: Following 2D classification, 734,850 particles were 3D-classified in Relion3 with C1 symmetry.
source: Following 2D classification, 734,850 particles were 3D-classified in Relion3 with C1 symmetry (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) (Scheres, 2012).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the image processing procedure.

claim: All classes showed that the voltage sensors were oriented with Fabs projecting towards the extracellular face of the channel.
source: All classes showed that the voltage sensors were oriented with Fabs projecting towards the extracellular face of the channel.
evidence: This is an observation from the 3D classification results.

claim: The extracellular orientation of Fabs is compatible with the extracellular accessibility of these Fabs in electrophysiological studies.
source: This orientation is compatible with the extracellular accessibility of these Fabs in electrophysiological studies (Jiang et al., 2003b).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the structural observation to previous functional data.

claim: The extracellular orientation of Fabs in cryo-EM images contrasts with the non-native orientation of KvAP voltage sensors in crystal structures of the full-length channel.
source: The extracellular orientation of Fabs in cryo-EM images contrasts with the non-native orientation of KvAP voltage sensors in crystal structures of the full-length channel, in which detergents more dispersive than digitonin were used (Jiang et al., 2003a; Lee et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a comparison between the current cryo-EM structure and previous crystal structures.

claim: The precise positioning of the Fabs was variable.
source: While the Fabs were on the extracellular surface in all 3D classes, the precise positioning of the Fabs was variable, as shown (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is an observation from the 3D classification results.

claim: The positional variability of Fabs explains why in both 2D and 3D classes, density for the four Fabs is not constant.
source: The positional variability explains why in both 2D (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B) and 3D classes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3C), density for the four Fabs is not constant: in some classes only a single Fab is well aligned, in others 2, 3, or least frequently 4 Fabs are aligned.
evidence: This is an inference explaining the observed variability in Fab density.

claim: The variation in Fab orientation is consistent with past studies showing the high degree of mobility of the S3b-S4 paddle region of the voltage sensor.
source: The variation in Fab orientation is consistent with past studies showing the high degree of mobility of the S3b-S4 paddle region of the voltage sensor (Ruta et al., 2005; Butterwick and MacKinnon, 2010).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the observed variability to previous studies.

claim: The final density map was calculated to 6 Å resolution.
source: The final density map, calculated to 6 Å resolution, showed continuous density for the transmembrane region, density for the Fabs on the extracellular side and a poorly resolved cytoplasmic domain (CTD) on the intracellular side (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a description of the final cryo-EM map.

claim: The final density map showed continuous density for the transmembrane region.
source: The final density map, calculated to 6 Å resolution, showed continuous density for the transmembrane region, density for the Fabs on the extracellular side and a poorly resolved cytoplasmic domain (CTD) on the intracellular side (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a description of the final cryo-EM map.

claim: The final density map showed density for the Fabs on the extracellular side.
source: The final density map, calculated to 6 Å resolution, showed continuous density for the transmembrane region, density for the Fabs on the extracellular side and a poorly resolved cytoplasmic domain (CTD) on the intracellular side (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a description of the final cryo-EM map.

claim: The final density map showed a poorly resolved cytoplasmic domain (CTD) on the intracellular side.
source: The final density map, calculated to 6 Å resolution, showed continuous density for the transmembrane region, density for the Fabs on the extracellular side and a poorly resolved cytoplasmic domain (CTD) on the intracellular side (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a description of the final cryo-EM map.

claim: The existence of the cytoplasmic domain, formed by an extension of the C-terminus, was predicted from protein synthesis studies of KvAP.
source: The existence of the cytoplasmic domain, formed by an extension of the C-terminus, was predicted from protein synthesis studies of KvAP (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C) (McDonald et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to McDonald et al., 2019.

claim: The crystal structure of the isolated voltage sensor conforms well to the experimental cryo-EM map.
source: A model corresponding to the crystal structure of the isolated voltage sensor, unmodified, was placed into the density (Figure 2A,B) (Jiang et al., 2003a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fit of the crystal structure into the cryo-EM density.

claim: The crystal structure of the pore conforms well to the experimental cryo-EM map.
source: A model corresponding to the crystal structure of the pore, unmodified, was also placed into the density (Figure 2C,D) (Jiang et al., 2003a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fit of the crystal structure into the cryo-EM density.

claim: KvAP is a non-domain-swapped voltage-gated ion channel, meaning each voltage sensor is contiguous with the pore element from the same polypeptide chain.
source: An important first conclusion is that KvAP is a non-domain-swapped voltage-gated ion channel, meaning each voltage sensor is contiguous with the pore element from the same polypeptide chain (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is the primary structural finding of the study.

claim: The short turn connecting S4 to S5 instead of a long α-helical S4-S5 linker indicates that KvAP is non-domain-swapped.
source: That this must be the case is evident in the short turn connecting S4 to S5 instead of a long α-helical S4-S5 linker (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an inference from the structural observation.

claim: KvAP is topologically like Kv10-12 channels and unlike Kv1-7 channels.
source: Therefore, KvAP is topologically like Kv10-12 channels and unlike Kv1-7 channels (Figures 1 and 2E).
evidence: This is a comparison based on the structural finding.

claim: The voltage sensors in KvAP and eag1 orient differently with respect to the pore.
source: Figure 3 highlights a notable structural difference between KvAP and eag1 (Kv10) even though they both share a non-domain-swapped topology. Viewed from the extracellular side, their voltage sensors orient differently with respect to the pore, as shown (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a structural comparison shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In eag1, S1 contacts S5 near the extracellular surface, but is displaced about 15 Å away from S5 near the intracellular surface.
source: In eag1, S1 contacts S5 near the extracellular surface, but is displaced about 15 Å away from S5 near the intracellular surface (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the eag1 structure.

claim: In KvAP, S1 runs parallel to and in contact with S5 throughout its length inside the membrane.
source: In contrast, S1 in KvAP runs parallel to and in contact with S5 throughout its length inside the membrane (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the KvAP structure.

claim: EPR data on amino acid side-chain accessibility and mobility in membrane-embedded KvAP channels support the S1-S5 contact observed in the cryo-EM structure.
source: Perozo and co-workers analyzed amino acid side-chain accessibility and mobility in membrane-embedded KvAP channels using EPR (Cuello et al., 2004). Their data, which we have mapped onto the structure of KvAP, support the S1-S5 contact observed (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a comparison between the cryo-EM structure and previous EPR data.

claim: A continuous surface of low side-chain mobility and low O2 collision frequency is observed where S1 contacts S5 in the cryo-EM structure.
source: Specifically, a continuous surface of low side-chain mobility and low O2 collision frequency, which are both signatures of a buried protein surface, is observed where S1 contacts S5 in the cryo-EM structure.
evidence: This is an observation from mapping EPR data onto the structure.

claim: Low side-chain mobility and low O2 collision frequency are signatures of a buried protein surface.
source: Specifically, a continuous surface of low side-chain mobility and low O2 collision frequency, which are both signatures of a buried protein surface, is observed where S1 contacts S5 in the cryo-EM structure.
evidence: This is established knowledge about protein structure.

claim: The cryo-EM structure is consistent with the EPR data.
source: Altogether, the cryo-EM structure is consistent with the EPR data.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the structure with EPR data.

claim: The consistency between the cryo-EM structure and EPR data suggests that the cryo-EM structure is representative of a conformation of KvAP inside lipid bilayers.
source: This consistency suggests that the cryo-EM structure is representative of a conformation of KvAP inside lipid bilayers.
evidence: This is an inference from the consistency between structure and EPR data.

claim: In electrophysiological studies on KvAP, the membrane must be depolarized first before the extracellularly-applied Fabs can bind.
source: In electrophysiological studies on KvAP, the membrane must be depolarized first before the extracellularly-applied Fabs can bind (Jiang et al., 2003b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2003b.

claim: In the structure, the helical turn of S3b into S4, the Fab epitope, is exposed to the extracellular surface.
source: In the structure, the helical turn of S3b into S4, the Fab epitope, is exposed to the extracellular surface, compatible with Fab accessibility and a depolarized conformation of KvAP.
evidence: This is a structural observation.

claim: The exposure of the Fab epitope to the extracellular surface is compatible with Fab accessibility and a depolarized conformation of KvAP.
source: In the structure, the helical turn of S3b into S4, the Fab epitope, is exposed to the extracellular surface, compatible with Fab accessibility and a depolarized conformation of KvAP.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the structural observation to functional data.

claim: The voltage sensor is similar in conformation to depolarized voltage sensors in other voltage-gated ion channels.
source: The voltage sensor is similar in conformation to depolarized voltage sensors in other voltage-gated ion channels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a structural comparison shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Because of the unique interaction between S1 and S5, the S3b-S4 paddle in KvAP resides on the outer-most perimeter of the channel, oriented tangent to the pore domain.
source: However, because of the unique interaction between S1 and S5, the S3b-S4 paddle in KvAP resides on the outer-most perimeter of the channel, oriented tangent to the pore domain.
evidence: This is a structural observation and inference.

claim: The pore is less open than in the crystal structure of the full-length channel, but more open than in other closed K+ channels.
source: The pore is less open than in the crystal structure of the full-length channel, but more open than in other closed K+ channels (Figure 2D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2) (Jiang et al., 2003a; Tao et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a structural comparison with previous structures.

claim: KvAP opens and then inactivates partially following membrane depolarization.
source: Functionally, KvAP opens and then inactivates partially following membrane depolarization (Schmidt et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schmidt et al., 2009.

claim: The conformation of the inner helix gate in this structure might reflect a mixture of open and inactivated channels.
source: The conformation of the inner helix gate in this structure might reflect a mixture of open and inactivated channels.
evidence: This is speculation about the conformational state.

claim: With a 1 Å length tether, only superficial sites near the aqueous surfaces are accessible, except at two positions on the S4 helix.
source: With a 1 Å length tether, only superficial sites near the aqueous surfaces are accessible, except at two positions, shown as blue spheres for intracellular accessibility, on the S4 helix.
evidence: This is a description of previous biotin-avidin accessibility data mapped onto the structure.

claim: Two outlier positions on S4 are more than 15 Å away from the intracellular surface.
source: These outlier positions on the structure are more than 15 Å away from the intracellular surface.
evidence: This is a measurement from the structure.

claim: The accessibility assay result implies that the KvAP voltage sensor can undergo very large voltage-dependent conformational changes to bring these positions close to the intracellular surface.
source: But the accessibility assay was carried out in membranes under voltage clamp. The result implies that the KvAP voltage sensor can undergo very large voltage-dependent conformational changes to bring these positions close to the intracellular surface.
evidence: This is an inference from the accessibility data.

claim: Experiments using longer tethers show results consistent with shorter tethers.
source: Experiments using longer tethers show results consistent with shorter tethers. Specifically, positions on S4 become exposed to both the extracellular and intracellular sides, depending on the membrane voltage (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of previous accessibility data.

claim: Positions on S4 become exposed to both the extracellular and intracellular sides, depending on the membrane voltage.
source: Specifically, positions on S4 become exposed to both the extracellular and intracellular sides, depending on the membrane voltage (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of previous accessibility data.

claim: KvAP is an outlier among voltage-gated ion channels in the distribution of positive-charged amino acids on S4.
source: KvAP is an outlier among voltage-gated ion channels, whether domain-swapped or not, in two respects. First, the distribution of positive-charged amino acids on S4 is unique.
evidence: This is a comparison of KvAP's S4 sequence with other channels.

claim: In other Kv channels the region of S4 that contains gating charge residues consists of the strict triplet (RXX)n, where R (arginine) is sometimes replaced by K (lysine) and X stands for a hydrophobic amino acid.
source: In other Kv channels the region of S4 that contains gating charge residues – the active region – consists of the strict triplet (RXX)n, where R (arginine) is sometimes replaced by K (lysine) and X stands for a hydrophobic amino acid.
evidence: This is established knowledge about S4 sequences in Kv channels.

claim: The S4 sequence in KvAP shows a discontinuity between the fourth and fifth arginine residues created by six consecutive uncharged amino acids.
source: But consider the S4 sequence in KvAP: (RLV)(RLL)(RFL)(RIL)(LII)(SRG)(SKF). Here, we observe a discontinuity between the fourth and fifth arginine residues created by six consecutive uncharged amino acids; this produces a phase shift of the fifth and sixth (lysine) with respect to the first four.
evidence: This is an analysis of the KvAP S4 sequence.

claim: The fifth R and the following lysine in the KvAP S4 sequence are part of the active region of S4.
source: The fifth R as well as the following lysine in the sequence are certainly part of the active region of S4, because in the structure the lysine resides inside the gating charge transfer center (Figure 5C), which is the site at the center of the voltage sensor that lowers the energy barrier for charged amino acids as they cross the membrane (Tao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference from the structural position of the lysine.

claim: The gating charge transfer center is the site at the center of the voltage sensor that lowers the energy barrier for charged amino acids as they cross the membrane.
source: The fifth R as well as the following lysine in the sequence are certainly part of the active region of S4, because in the structure the lysine resides inside the gating charge transfer center (Figure 5C), which is the site at the center of the voltage sensor that lowers the energy barrier for charged amino acids as they cross the membrane (Tao et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tao et al., 2010.

claim: In other voltage-gated ion channels, S4 adopts a 310 helix at the center of the membrane.
source: In other voltage-gated ion channels, S4 adopts a 310 helix at the center of the membrane; this secondary structure directs the arginine residues towards the gating charge transfer center.
evidence: This is established knowledge about S4 structure in voltage-gated channels.

claim: The 310 helix secondary structure directs the arginine residues towards the gating charge transfer center.
source: In other voltage-gated ion channels, S4 adopts a 310 helix at the center of the membrane; this secondary structure directs the arginine residues towards the gating charge transfer center.
evidence: This is established knowledge about S4 structure in voltage-gated channels.

claim: Because triplet periodicity is not maintained over the lower half of S4 in KvAP, it is not entirely clear whether properties learned from other Kv channels apply to KvAP.
source: Because triplet periodicity is not maintained over the lower half of S4 in KvAP, it is not entirely clear whether properties learned from other Kv channels apply to KvAP.
evidence: This is speculation about the implications of the unique S4 sequence.

claim: KvAP is an outlier among voltage-gated ion channels in the composition of the gating charge transfer center.
source: The second respect in which KvAP is an outlier concerns the gating charge transfer center. KvAP has the typical constellation of negative-charged amino acids to stabilize the positive charge on arginine or lysine. But instead of the phenylalanine found in other Kv channels (357 out of 360 examined), KvAP contains a leucine.
evidence: This is a comparison of KvAP's gating charge transfer center with other channels.

claim: 357 out of 360 examined Kv channels contain a phenylalanine in the gating charge transfer center.
source: But instead of the phenylalanine found in other Kv channels (357 out of 360 examined), KvAP contains a leucine.
evidence: This is a statistical observation from sequence analysis.

claim: KvAP contains a leucine instead of phenylalanine in the gating charge transfer center.
source: But instead of the phenylalanine found in other Kv channels (357 out of 360 examined), KvAP contains a leucine.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the KvAP structure.

claim: The functional significance of the leucine in KvAP's gating charge transfer center is unknown.
source: The functional significance of this is also unknown.
evidence: Explicitly stated as unknown.

claim: The HCN channel has been captured in both depolarized and hyperpolarized conformations.
source: In separate studies in our lab, we have captured the HCN channel, another non-domain-swapped voltage-gated channel, in both depolarized and hyperpolarized conformations (Lee and MacKinnon, 2017; Lee and MacKinnon, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lee and MacKinnon, 2017 and 2019.

claim: When depolarized, the voltage sensor in HCN is similar to that in KvAP.
source: When depolarized, the voltage sensor in HCN is similar to that in KvAP.
evidence: This is a structural comparison.

claim: When hyperpolarized, the S4 helix in HCN translates toward the cytoplasm and breaks into an L-shape, with the bottom half of S4 forming an interfacial helix.
source: But when hyperpolarized, the S4 helix translates toward the cytoplasm and breaks into an L-shape, with the bottom half of S4 forming an interfacial helix.
evidence: This is a description of the hyperpolarized HCN structure.

claim: The voltage sensor in HCN couples to the gate in a fundamentally different manner than in domain-swapped voltage-gated channels studied so far.
source: Thus, the voltage sensor in HCN couples to the gate in a fundamentally different manner than in domain-swapped voltage-gated channels studied so far, where the S4-S5 linker forms a permanent interfacial helix (Figure 1C).
